L365@P17: dramatic consequences for our understanding of art history. For example, the idea
L366@P17: that Vermeer had expressed ‘a deep religious emotion’ in the painting Christ and his
L367@P17: Disciples at Emmaus became instantly obsolete when this painting was exposed as a
L368@P17: fake in 1947.2 (fig. 1.1)
L369@P17:  Despite the complexity and importance of attributions, however, little
L370@P17: theory has been devoted to connoisseurship. Within academic art history, hardly
L371@P17: any methodology has been developed to attribute Dutch and Flemish old master
L372@P17: paintings. There is no handbook that could help train aspiring connoisseurs, and
L373@P17: only a few connoisseurs have ever published coherent views on their working
L374@P17: methods. Moreover, no survey exists on the developments in this field in the
L375@P17: relatively recent past.3 This essay presents a brief overview of the insights which
L376@P17: have been developed in the field of Dutch and Flemish painting since the end of
L377@P17: the Second World War. It is far from exhaustive and is based only on published
L378@P17: sources. The main questions are: How have the various experts defined and
L379@P17: redefined the process of attributing paintings from this period? What new
L380@P17: techniques have been developed, and how do these affect the experts’ views on
L381@P17: the attribution process? Can this process be captured in a rational method, or
L382@P17: does it ultimately defy definition? And what specific attribution issues have caused
L383@P17: debate among experts in recent years?

L388@P17-18: by Catherine B. Scallen. See Scallen 2004. 18 THE FINGERPRINT OF AN OLD MASTER
L389@P18: The Van Meegeren Scandal: A Turning Point
L390@P18: Almost immediately after the Second World War, art historians and laymen alike
L391@P18: began to question the ability of experts of seventeenth-century Dutch art to
L392@P18: attribute paintings with an unprecedented force. Their doubt was the result of a
L393@P18: remarkable lawsuit in 1945-47, the Van Meegeren case, which marks a turning
L394@P18: point in the history of modern connoisseurship. During this trial, the painting
L395@P18: Christ and his Disciples at Emmaus, which was widely celebrated as one of Vermeer’s
L396@P18: best paintings, turned out to be a forgery (fig. 1.1 Han van Meegeren, Christ and his
L397@P18: Disciples at Emmaus, c. 1937, Museum Boymans-van Beuningen).
L398@P18: In 1937 the piece had been ‘rediscovered’ by the well-known art historian
L399@P18: Abraham Bredius, and the Boijmans-van Beuningen Museum in Rotterdam had
L400@P18: been quick to purchase it (with the help of Bredius himself who donated 10.000
L401@P18: guilders towards the acquisition). Although Bredius had initially had some doubts
L402@P18: about the provenance and attribution of the painting, he had concluded that it was
L403@P18: ‘authentic’ after completing a brief background check on the seller and closely
L404@P18: inspecting the painting in July 1937.4 He subsequently wrote an article about the
L405@P18: piece for the prestigious art historical monthly The Burlington Magazine, in which he
L406@P18: celebrated the painting as Vermeer’s best work.5 Other experts followed suit. The
L407@P18: composition was said to be well-balanced, the colours exquisite, the still life better
L408@P18: than any other from the period, Christ’s face ‘filled with secrecy’ (Knuttel, 1938);
L409@P18: and the maid ‘perhaps the most beautiful one Vermeer ever painted’ (Van
L410@P18: Thienen, 1939). Moreover, the style of the work was said to express all the great
L411@P18: character traits of the painter himself (Hefting, 1938).6
L412@P18:  Most experts only started to voice doubts about the authenticity of the
L413@P18: painting during the two-year long lawsuit against the master forger Han van
L414@P18: Meegeren, which started a few weeks after the end of World War II. Initially, Van
L415@P18: Meegeren was sued for treason. He was thought to have taken advantage of the
L416@P18: war situation in the Netherlands in 1943 to illegitimately sell a Vermeer, The
L417@P18: Adulteress, to an agent of the German marshal Hermann Göring without
L418@P18: permission to export such an important piece of the Dutch cultural heritage (fig.
L419@P18: 1.2). However, Van Meegeren denied the accusation, stating that he had not sold

L440@P19:  ‘In my personal opinion I would like to state that it is completely
L441@P19: unacceptable that this work, which has no equal in Dutch painting in its pure
L442@P19: expression of a deep religious emotion, would have been painted by a cowardish
L443@P19: cheater […] If this work is indeed old, Vermeer would be the only painter who

L446@P19:  Such a position became increasingly difficult to maintain. To add
L447@P19: credibility to his claim, Van Meegeren decided to create a new Vermeer forgery
L448@P19: during the trial. Meanwhile, a variety of evidence surfaced. In Van Meegeren’s
L449@P19: workshop in France, the police found a painting in the style of Vermeer, one in
L450@P19: the style of Pieter de Hooch, as well as a part of the seventeenth-century stretcher
L451@P19: on which Christ and his Disciples at Emmaus had been painted. (Van Meegeren
L452@P19: claimed he had altered the width of the stretcher to fit his composition.) Also, for
L453@P19: none of the paintings mentioned by Van Meegeren could a provenance history be
L454@P19: established.
L455@P19: When a number of painting experts were consulted in court – prof. Dr.
L456@P19: Johan Q. van Regteren Altena, dr. Hans Schneider, dr. Wiebo Froentjes, prof. Dr.
L457@P19: Paul Coremans, Dr. Harold J. Plenderleith, mr. F. Ian G. Rawlins, and dr.

L460@P19: kunst wordt overtroffen, geschilderd zou zijn door een laffen spotter en leugenaar, met het plan er
L461@P19: een dergelijk laag bedrog mee te plegen. […] Als het schilderij werkelijk oud is, is Vermeer m.i. de

L463@P19-20: dit boek op zijn plaats.’ Bremer 1945, foreword; see also Van Dantzig, 1947, 61. 20 THE FINGERPRINT OF AN OLD MASTER
L464@P20: Angenitus M. Wild – they stated that the suspicious works did not date from the
L465@P20: time of Vermeer and De Hoogh, and that these works could indeed have been
L466@P20: painted by Van Meegeren.8 [Interestingly, Van Regteren Altena had recognized
L467@P20: the painting as authentic in 1938, but since then changed his mind.9] Scientific
L468@P20: tests executed by Dr. Coremans confirmed a curious characteristic of the forger’s
L469@P20: working method. According to his own explanation, Van Meegeren always created
L470@P20: his forgeries on top of seventeenth-century paintings and used pigments that were
L471@P20: consistent with those used by the old masters; however, unlike seventeenthcentury painters, he did not use oil paint. Instead, he had chosen for a modern
L472@P20: type of binding medium, ‘bakelite’ (phenol-formaldehyde), which allowed him to
L473@P20: imitate the cracked surface of centuries old oil paintings by briefly baking the
L474@P20: finished paintings in an oven. This binding medium had only been invented in
L475@P20: 1907 and thus proved that the paintings could not have been made in the
L476@P20: seventeenth-century.10
L477@P20:  For legal reasons, it was not necessary to further analyse the stylistic
L478@P20: interpretations of Christ and his Disciples at Emmaus. But it was certainly curious that
L479@P20: the Boijmans painting had been analysed in such radically different ways. Both
L480@P20: before and immediately after the trial experts described the style of Christ and his
L481@P20: Disciples at Emmaus in quite generic terms strongly infused with value judgements.
L482@P20: Interestingly, some of the same elements that were initially used to underline the
L483@P20: quality of the work were later seen as illustrative of the work’s deficiencies. After
L484@P20: the trial, the composition was seen as unbalanced and rather forced, the colours
L485@P20: too grey, Christ’s face decidedly effeminate (Kilbracken, 1967), the maid crosseyed and bald, and her lips too thick (Van Dantzig, 1947).11
L486@P20: This radical shift in appreciation was somewhat softened by voices who
L487@P20: claimed that a number of scholars had recognized the Boijmans painting as a
L488@P20: forgery long before the Van Meegeren trial had started.12 However, the published

L310@P6-7: 246 The Stylistic Detection of Forgeries
L311@P7: T H E O D O R E R 0 U S S E A U Chairman of the European Paintings Department
L312@P7: THIS SEMINAR, devoted to the detection of forgeries
L313@P7: by stylistic analysis, and the next one, on scientific methods of detection, should be thought of together, for they
L314@P7: are complementary and one can't stand independently
L315@P7: of the other. Modern science has brought us new techniques of analyzing works of art that reinforce and are a
L316@P7: considerable help to the stylistic methods that have
L317@P7: existed for a long time, which we will discuss here this
L318@P7: evening.
L319@P7: I'll begin by trying to give you an idea of what we
L320@P7: mean by style. This is a very subtle and complex matter,
L321@P7: and therefore an extremely difficult one to present to
L322@P7: a large audience, but I thought the best way to do it
L323@P7: would be to discuss a well-known forgery. First, a word of
L324@P7: warning: we should all realize that we can only talk about
L325@P7: the bad forgeries, the ones that have been detected; the
L326@P7: good ones are still hanging on the walls. A sense of humor
L327@P7: is important in this subject, and so is common sense and
L328@P7: the realization that there aren't so many forgeries, discovered or undiscovered, as the newspapers would like
L329@P7: to make us believe. Forgeries are exceptional at any
L330@P7: time. They're created by a market: if the market's good
L331@P7: there are more than when the market is quiet.
L332@P7: To get back to my subject, the forgery that I'm going
L333@P7: to talk about is an exceptional one, because it was considered a beautiful thing-and forgeries rarely are. One
L334@P7: of the characteristics of average forgeries, the kind we've
L335@P7: heard about recently, is that they're mediocre. That is
L336@P7: why they pass: they escape notice. But this one was
L337@P7: thought to be very fine: it is the picture of Christ and
L338@P7: the Pilgrims at Emmaus (Figure I), attributed to Vermeer but actually painted by Han van Meegeren, the
L339@P7: Dutch forger who flourished just before and during the
L340@P7: Second World War.
L341@P7: I'll start by pointing out the reasons for this picture's
L342@P7: success, the things in it that were done well. Then I'm
L343@P7: going to show you a painting by Vermeer. By comparing
L344@P7: the stylistic qualities of the two, we can draw our conclusions.
L345@P7: The key to the whole question of van Meegeren's
L346@P7: success is that he did not try to imitate the classical
L347@P7: Vermeer - the Vermeer we all think of, in the pictures
L348@P7: upstairs and in the Rijksmuseum and other great galleries. Van Meegeren chose Vermeer because he was a
L349@P7: Dutchman, because he was famous, and because his
L350@P7: works are very rare and very expensive. At the time van
L351@P7: Meegeren began, there were rumors all over Europe that
L352@P7: Andrew Mellon had offered more than one million
L353@P7: dollars-an enormous sum in those days, much greater
L354@P7: than it is today-for the famous Artist in His Studio,
L355@P7: now in the Vienna museum, which was then still in private hands. Van Meegeren, who had studied and knew
L356@P7: art history, took advantage of the fact that Vermeer's a
L357@P7: man we know little about. We have a group of works
L358@P7: done when Vermeer was mature, some of which are
L359@P7: dated. The work of his youth is missing. We have three
L360@P7: or four pictures that we believe were painted when he
L361@P7: was young. They are quite different; so different that
L362@P7: the one in Figure 2, Christ in the House of Mary and
L363@P7: Martha, in the Edinburgh museum, would not, I believe, have been attributed to him if it were not for
L364@P7: the fact that it bears his signature. (Even with the signature, it has taken people a long time to accept it as
L365@P7: his.) In other words, part of Vermeer's oeuvre is missing. Well, van Meegeren saw this gap and decided that
L366@P7: he would fill it. He wouldn't copy Vermeer: he would
L367@P7: create the missing part of Vermeer's oeuvre.
L368@P7: Every forger, when he paints, has to begin by getting
L369@P7: a feeling for the period and the place in which the picture is supposed to have been painted. Van Meegeren
L370@P7: has captured this feeling to some extent in the Pilgrims
L371@P7: at Emmaus. The simplicity of the background and the
L372@P7: architecture, the solemn, Protestant atmosphere, fit our
L373@P7: idea of seventeenth-century Holland. The way the bulk
L374@P7: of the figures fills the picture is a seventeenth-century

L449@P10: figure. There is a sentimentality to the head of Christ
L450@P10: that is quite foreign to anything of the real Vermeer.
L451@P10: It's actually much closer to our time. This is a major
L452@P10: weakness of any forger: he can't help interpreting past
L453@P10: art in terms of present predilections. The modeling is
L454@P10: not done in a series of facets, and the touch is greasy,
L455@P10: without that wonderful cool and measured quality that
L456@P10: you get in Vermeer. The overall harmony and balance
L457@P10: of Vermeer's pictures is also missing: look at van Meegeren's exaggerations, his insistence on the seams on the
L458@P10: sleeves and the highlights on the bread-impossible for
L459@P10: Vermeer.
L460@P10: In spite of these faults, van Meegeren was almost
L461@P10: successful. But he was almost successful not because of
L462@P10: the painting-I think that is plain, although stylistic

L464@P12: art -but because of the tricks he played. He was a remarkable confidence man, an extremely intelligent
L465@P12: crook. He created a provenance for the picture; he had
L466@P12: an intermediary who sold it for him; he got one of the
L467@P12: most prominent art historians-Abraham Bredius-to
L468@P12: write an article on it, which was published in The Burlington Magazine; it was then exhibited publicly. Finally
L469@P12: it was sold to the Boymans museum. The museum hesitated about taking it, although they were urged by
L470@P12: D. G. van Beuningen, an important collector who later
L471@P12: bought others of van Meegeren's works. In the end, the
L472@P12: museum was pushed into buying it because van Meegeren floated the rumor that the Rijksmuseum wanted
L473@P12: to get it.
L474@P12: At the end of the war I interrogated one of Goring's
L475@P12: agents, a man who represented him in Holland. It was
L476@P12: he who bought, or was the intermediary for Giring's
L477@P12: purchase of, a picture by van Meegeren after war was
L478@P12: declared. This man, Alois Miedel, told me the story of
L479@P12: how this happened, an instance of van Meegeren's astute
L480@P12: sense of timing and his exploitation of circumstance.
L481@P12: Miedel ran a small bank in Amsterdam. His wife was
L482@P12: Jewish, and they finally fled from Holland to Spain,
L483@P12: where I found and interrogated Miedel himself. He told
L484@P12: me he aided the Resistance under cover all through the
L485@P12: war, helping people to escape, out of loyalty to his Jewish wife. One night a man, who, he knew, was in the
L486@P12: Resistance, came to him and said, "Mr. Miedel, I know
L487@P12: you buy paintings for the Reichsmarschall and I have a
L488@P12: picture for you. But I will sell it to you only on one condition, and that is that you don't inquire where it came
L489@P12: from, because it belongs to an old Dutch family who
L490@P12: want to give the money to the Resistance." At that time
L491@P12: Miedel had staying with him an old friend, Heinrich
L492@P12: Hoffmann, Hitler's photographer and advisor on artistic

L494@P12: Miedel took the painting up to Hoffmann, who said,
